summary: Creates an IANA registry for SIP header field parameters and parameter values, and lists the existing ones as initial entries.

plainLanguage.summary: It starts an official list so no two people give the same name to different SIP settings, and fills it with the names already in use.

subtitle: The official list that keeps SIP header field parameter names from colliding.

tldr.problem: SIP lets people define new header field parameters and parameter values, but RFC 3261 never created an IANA registry for them, so names could clash.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3968 creates a sub-registry of SIP header field parameters under the SIP Parameters registry. Anything registered must be defined in an RFC, and the registry starts with the parameters that already exist.
tldr.outcome: Registered parameters become reserved words that implementations must use as their defining RFC describes. The document also updates RFC 3427.

facts.label: Required per entry
facts.value: Header field, parameter name, predefined values flag, RFC reference

today: RFC 3968 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 98) and nothing in its metadata marks it as obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 3427 and builds on the registry framework of RFC 3261.

sections.title: Why a Parameter Registry
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) lets people define new header field parameters and new values for them. RFC 3261 allows this but left out an IANA registry for them. RFC 3968 creates that registry.

It also updates RFC 3427, which documents the process for extending SIP, by saying how to define and register new header field parameters and parameter values. The document uses the requirement words MUST, SHOULD and MAY as defined in BCP 14.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP messages have little labelled settings. Nobody kept a master list of the labels, so this RFC starts one.

sections.title: Rules for Using the Registry
sections.content:
A SIP header field parameter or parameter value MUST be documented in an RFC before IANA will register it. The RFC MUST fully explain the syntax, intended usage and semantics. The goal is interoperability between independent implementations and no accidental name collisions between dissimilar features. Unlike other protocol registries, this one has no vendor-extension tree, because RFC 3427 raises concerns that new extensions may damage security or greatly increase the complexity of the protocol.

RFCs that define parameters MUST register them. Registered names are treated as reserved words: they MUST be used consistently with their defining RFC, and implementations MUST NOT use private or locally defined parameters that conflict with registered ones.

Unregistered parameters may still be used, but the RFC warns this is risky: a new registration can appear at any time and may conflict with one already in use.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want a name in the book, you must first write down exactly what it means. Once a name is in the book, nobody may use it for something else.

sections.title: What a Registry Entry Contains
sections.content:
The registry is a sub-registry under the SIP Parameters registry that section 27 of RFC 3261 created for method names, header field names, warning codes, status codes and option tags. A registration MUST give four things: the header field the parameter appears in, the parameter name, whether the parameter accepts only a set of predefined values, and a reference to the RFC that defines it (plus any RFC that defines new values).

Parameters in different header fields MAY share a name. Parameters in the same header field MUST have different names.

Parameter values are registered by reference rather than in their own sub-registries. For a parameter marked Yes in the predefined-values column, implementers must read the referenced RFCs to find all valid values. References to RFCs that define values appear in double brackets, as with [[RFC 3310]] for the algorithm parameter.

The initial contents cover many header fields, including Accept, Authorization, Contact, From, To, Via, Reason, Security-Client and the P-header families, mostly pointing at RFC 3261 and a handful of other RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry is a card with four lines: where the setting lives, its name, whether it has a fixed menu of choices, and which RFC explains it.

sections.title: Registration Policy
sections.content: Using the terminology of RFC 2434, the policy for SIP header field parameters and parameter values is IETF Consensus. The parameter or value MUST be defined by an RFC, but that RFC does not have to be on the standards track.
sections.plainLanguage: To get into the book, the community has to agree and the idea has to be written up in an RFC. It does not have to be the most official kind.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The registry itself has no security considerations. However, as RFC 3427 notes, an important reason for the IETF to manage SIP extensions is to ensure that all extensions and parameters can be used securely. The RFCs that support parameter registrations MUST give detailed security considerations for them.
sections.plainLanguage: The book is harmless, but anyone adding a new entry has to explain how to use it safely.
